subject: biology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In semi-conservative replication, each new DNA molecule consists of:
options: Fragments of both original strands recombined
One original strand and one new strand
questions.explain: Each daughter molecule conserves one parental strand which acts as a template for one newly synthesised strand.

questions.q: The reduction division that halves the chromosome number occurs at which point in meiosis?
options: meiosis I, when homologous chromosomes separate
questions.explain: Meiosis I is the reduction division: homologous chromosomes are separated, halving the chromosome number from diploid to haploid.

questions.q: Crossing over during meiosis:
options: reduces the chromosome number to haploid
occurs in anaphase II between sister chromatids
involves exchange of alleles between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes at the chiasmata
questions.explain: In prophase I, non-sister chromatids of a homologous pair exchange equivalent sections at chiasmata, producing new allele combinations.

questions.q: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER) differs in function from RER in that the SER:
options: synthesises and transports lipids and steroids and stores calcium ions
questions.explain: The SER lacks ribosomes and is involved in lipid and steroid synthesis, plus calcium ion storage, rather than protein synthesis.

questions.q: The genetic code is described as 'degenerate'. This means that:
options: Some codons do not code for any amino acid
Most amino acids can be coded for by more than one codon
Each codon codes for more than one amino acid
questions.explain: Degeneracy means most amino acids are specified by more than one triplet codon.

questions.q: Why can a light microscope not resolve two ribosomes that are 25 nm apart?
options: light has too short a wavelength
the resolving power of a light microscope (about 200 nm) is limited by the wavelength of visible light, which is far larger than 25 nm
ribosomes are too large to be seen
questions.explain: Visible light's wavelength limits resolution to roughly 200 nm, so structures only 25 nm apart cannot be distinguished by a light microscope.

questions.q: The genetic code is universal. This means that:
options: A given codon codes for the same amino acid in almost all organisms
Each amino acid has only one codon
The code is read in overlapping triplets
Every codon codes for a different amino acid
questions.explain: Universality means the same codons specify the same amino acids across nearly all living organisms.

questions.q: The role of the nucleolus within the nucleus is to:
options: manufacture ribosomal RNA and assemble ribosome subunits
questions.explain: The nucleolus is the site of rRNA synthesis and the assembly of ribosomal subunits, which are then exported to the cytoplasm.

questions.q: During gel electrophoresis of DNA fragments, the fragments move towards the anode (positive electrode) because:
options: DNA carries an overall positive charge
Larger fragments are repelled by the gel
The phosphate groups give DNA an overall negative charge
questions.explain: The phosphate backbone gives DNA a net negative charge, so fragments migrate towards the positive anode.

questions.q: An organelle measured as 4.4 micrometres long appears 22 mm long in an electron micrograph. The magnification of the image is:
questions.explain: Magnification = image size / actual size = 22000 micrometres / 4.4 micrometres = 5000.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a feature of the genetic code?
questions.explain: The code is non-overlapping, not overlapping; each base is read as part of only one codon.

questions.q: A cell measures 30 mm in a photomicrograph taken at a magnification of x1500. The actual size of the cell is:
questions.explain: Actual size = image size / magnification = 30 mm / 1500 = 0.02 mm = 20 micrometres.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly describes the cell cycle?
questions.explain: Interphase comprises G1 (growth), S (DNA replication) and G2 (preparation), followed by mitosis and cytokinesis.

questions.q: The magnification and resolution of a microscope are different properties; resolution is best defined as:
options: how many times larger the image appears than the object
the minimum distance between two points at which they can still be distinguished as separate
the depth of field of the lens
questions.explain: Resolution is the ability to distinguish two close points as separate; it is limited by the wavelength of radiation used, not by magnification.

questions.q: Oestrogen affects gene expression by:
options: Binding to DNA polymerase to speed up replication
Methylating cytosine bases to silence genes
Binding to a receptor to form a transcription factor complex that switches on target genes
questions.explain: Oestrogen binds its receptor, and the complex acts as a transcription factor that initiates transcription of target genes.

questions.q: DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to the 3' end of a strand. This explains why:
options: The leading strand is synthesised in fragments
Helicase is required to join the fragments
The lagging strand is synthesised discontinuously as Okazaki fragments
questions.explain: Because synthesis must run 5' to 3', the antiparallel lagging strand is built discontinuously as Okazaki fragments later joined by ligase.

questions.q: The total magnification of a light microscope using a x10 eyepiece and a x40 objective lens is:
questions.explain: Total magnification is the product of the eyepiece and objective magnifications: 10 multiplied by 40 = 400.

questions.q: DNA ligase is required in recombinant DNA technology to:
options: Form phosphodiester bonds joining the DNA fragment into the vector
questions.explain: Ligase catalyses phosphodiester bond formation, sealing the inserted DNA into the vector backbone.

questions.q: Activated nucleotides used in DNA replication carry two extra phosphate groups. The breaking of these bonds:
options: Removes errors from the new strand
Releases energy that drives the condensation reaction joining nucleotides
questions.explain: Hydrolysis of the two additional phosphates releases energy that powers phosphodiester bond formation.

questions.q: Lysosomes contain hydrolytic enzymes whose role is to:
options: break down worn-out organelles, pathogens and cell debris
questions.explain: Lysosomes hold hydrolases that digest unwanted material and engulfed pathogens, recycling cellular components.

questions.q: Epigenetic modifications differ from mutations because they:
options: Change the sequence of DNA bases
Affect gene expression without changing the DNA base sequence
questions.explain: Epigenetic changes (e.g. methylation, acetylation) alter gene expression without altering the underlying base sequence.

questions.q: During translation, the bond formed between adjacent amino acids on the ribosome is a:
questions.explain: Amino acids are joined by peptide bonds in a condensation reaction catalysed at the ribosome.

questions.q: Increased methylation of DNA in a gene's promoter region typically results in:
options: A change in the DNA base sequence
questions.explain: Promoter methylation usually prevents transcription factor binding, inhibiting transcription without altering the base sequence.

questions.q: Meiosis produces:
questions.explain: Two successive divisions yield four haploid cells, each genetically unique due to crossing over and independent assortment.

questions.q: Ribosomes found free in the cytoplasm of a eukaryotic cell are:
options: made of pure protein with no RNA
bound only to the rough endoplasmic reticulum
70S, the same as in the mitochondrion's matrix
80S, larger than the 70S ribosomes of prokaryotes
questions.explain: Eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S, whereas prokaryotic and organellar ribosomes are the smaller 70S type.

questions.q: In eukaryotes, splicing of pre-mRNA involves:
options: Addition of a poly-A tail only
Removal of exons and joining of introns
Removal of introns and joining of exons
questions.explain: Splicing removes the non-coding introns and joins the exons together to produce mature mRNA.

questions.q: A feature found in some prokaryotic cells but never in eukaryotic cells is:
questions.explain: Plasmids, small circular loops of DNA separate from the main chromosome, are characteristic of prokaryotes and absent from eukaryotic cells.

questions.q: During the S phase of interphase, the key event is:
options: semi-conservative replication of DNA so each chromosome consists of two identical sister chromatids
questions.explain: In the synthesis (S) phase DNA is replicated, producing two identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere for each chromosome.

questions.q: A scanning electron microscope (SEM) is particularly useful for studying the surface of a pollen grain because it:
options: uses visible light to give true colour
scans the surface and detects reflected/secondary electrons to build a 3D image of surface topography
passes electrons through a thin section to show internal detail
questions.explain: An SEM scans the specimen surface, and detected secondary electrons produce a three-dimensional image of surface features.

questions.q: DNA replication is described as semi-conservative rather than conservative because experiments showed that after one round of replication in heavy then light isotopes, all DNA was:
options: A mixture of fully heavy and fully light molecules
Of intermediate density (one heavy strand, one light strand)
questions.explain: Meselson and Stahl found a single intermediate-density band after one generation, supporting semi-conservative replication.
